questions.answer: Personal connection to the destination (heritage / friends there/ etc.)

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
Metropolics. It's so convenient and diverse. 
School itself, I chose Paris 1 University because it shares a campus with the Sorbonne University, and the school is too beautiful.
The project itself. I've always been curious about finance and economics.

questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
It wasn't too difficult for me because I worked a summer job to prepare for renting an apartment in Paris, so I had a fairly generous budget. 

I found it on the Chinese social media app Xiaohongshu (Little Red Book), which was relatively easy to find since there are many Chinese people in Paris. I actually recommend it because there're so many houses, but be aware and careful of the scam. I know one Chinese student got scam for 4000 euros and he even saw the apartment himself in person. So be careful! I tried facebook as well and also airbnb but the location and price are way worse.

I also started looking for apartments two months in advance. And because I already have an EU residence permit, I didn't need to go through many formalities, like official address.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
I think you need to check if the appliances and heating in your room work, especially if you're renting a Haussmann building. Paris has many old, romantic Haussmann buildings, but they're only pretty to look at; living there long-term is miserable. For example, my apartment had limited power; if I turned on the heating and used a hairdryer, the circuit breaker would trip very quickly. I felt very cramped in the winter.

I strongly recommend that you live near the university. Public transportation in Paris is frequently problematic, and universities there are very strict, with high attendance requirements. Things are difficult to negotiate due to the somewhat chaotic management. Living close by will allow you to get everything done quickly and efficiently, which will be very beneficial.

Many older apartments in Paris do not have washing machines. If your rented apartment does not have a washing machine, check if there are any laundry facilities in the neighborhood.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
It was incredibly difficult; everyone was complaining so much that I don't want to recount the process. 

The credit hours and course schedules provided by the host institution were severely inconsistent with reality, and course capacity was extremely limited. They basically did nothing for two weeks, sending no emails or information, and then suddenly one evening they'd notify you to register for classes the next day. If you missed the email, you were on your own. 

Then, if you wanted to change courses, or if you absolutely had to (I had to change courses because one professor didn't want to speak English), it was practically impossible. The person in charge was almost never in the office, and it took a very long time to reply.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Church, so you can go and pray. After this I understand why there's security check at the entrance of the university, students could be very mad.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I successfully registered for about a third of the courses I wanted. The courses available for exchange students were extremely limited; excluding French courses and overlapping time slots, there were almost no options. The person in charge kept emphasizing that if I chose courses from other departments, he wouldn't be responsible for any related exam overlaps or other issues, so I was scared off choosing courses from other departments.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Make sure you check your email frequently and register as early as possible, ideally at the first minute, as it's first-come, first-served.

Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: It was very difficult. Because I had never studied economics, and although the course was called economics, the teaching method was very traditional, with a lot of math.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
Teachers frequently write on the blackboard by hand; almost everyone does. And compared to Copenhagen, the teachers' spoken English is generally not very good.

Many teachers don't allow photos of their PowerPoint presentations because they use those materials for exam questions, and they often don't reply to emails. Many classes don't have teaching assistants, so almost everything is self-taught.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: urban economics/ micro finance/ economics of education/ microeconomics: uncertainty and information/ resource and climate change/ economics of banking

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I recommend Microfinance, Banking Economics, and Microeconomics: Uncertainty and Information. The first two are FMBA courses, packed with information and very engaging. The last one is an undergraduate course that provides a lot of foundational knowledge about economics.

Additional comments:
questions.answer: Everything was in French, and registering for physical education classes was very confusing.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There was a cocktail party on the first day of school, and the desserts were delicious. There was also a buddy system where you could find a buddy, but it wasn't very useful.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
There's so much to do in Paris. I didn't participate much in the school's activities because I'm not particularly talkative. But I had a lot of great time on my own with friends.

Paris has many cinemas, and movie tickets are very cheap.

Museums and art galleries are almost all free for students.

Paris has so many delicious foods! There's a fusion tapas place called Otto near Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne University; their lunch sets are a great deal, highly recommended.

Paris also has many bars, and the cocktails are fantastic. The cafes are also excellent; their Korean and Japanese coffees are superb.

It might sound strange, but getting a haircut in Paris is very affordable and there are plenty of options.

Paris' parks are beautiful and perfect for sunbathing.

Paris is a great city for walking; it's not windy, everything has a historical atmosphere, and it's beautiful—take lots of photos.

Paris is a perfect city for romance. I highly recommend walking hand-in-hand with your partner along the Seine, strolling through the Marais district, and buying vintage clothing—Paris has a huge selection of vintage items.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: You could take a day trip to Versailles Palace, or attend the Montmartre Wine Festival. Keep an eye on social media for events. Or just chill: get a good sleep, have a long brunch, read or study in a beautiful library, stroll around the city, soak up the sun, enjoy a nice meal, meet friends, or watch a movie. There's so much to do in Paris. On weekends, you could also take the train to Nice or a bus to Belgium. Yes, Flixbus isn't just going to Germany anymore, haha.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It's easy. Paris is a very inclusive city. I don't think people need to adjust because Paris has almost everything, and Parisians are almost used to everything. You can always find a sense of belonging. Paris has enough space and freedom for you to be yourself.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: To be honest, no, because I met a lot of Chinese students, and I felt that the French didn't speak English very much, and their English wasn't very good either.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The school's administration is so chaotic, if that's what you call a cultural difference.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: People know how to relax, they don't love working, they don't have age anxiety, they are very inclusive, you can find almost any food or culture here, and strangers are friendly and will help with luggage. Ladies always go first. Everyone is well-dressed and very elegant.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Beware of thieves and pickpockets. Don't talk to strangers; that's how my phone was stolen. Don't rely on the police in Paris.

Finding accommodation in advance will give you many options.

Study hard. The academic workload in Paris is heavy, and all exams are closed-book, making it quite difficult and rigorous. The teachers will not make any exceptions for exchange students.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: It's best to learn French in advance.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: I would say that this exchange program has given me more confidence, even though I did terribly academically. However, I made many new friends, solved my own moving and housing problems, and learned new subjects. I feel I've grown a lot. And I've always wanted to live in Paris for a while, and that wish has come true.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: I would say the difficulties were loneliness, anxiety, and uncertainty. It was hard to make friends in a new country, and my classmates weren't very talkative. Studying was tough. Many things didn't go as planned because of the chaotic school management; sometimes I felt powerless. And I experienced racial discrimination and phone theft at the subway station; I felt traumatized, but I'm much better now.

Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
